title: The Big Secret of Dealing With People
coreMove: Name one specific, true, unflattery-free thing you appreciate about the person in front of you, and say it out loud before you ask for anything.

exampleSpecs.domain: a charge nurse on a 3 a.m. handoff thanking the orderly who re-stocked the crash cart without being asked
exampleSpecs.audience: a mid-career manager who habitually notices what goes wrong before what goes right
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the orderly keeps volunteering the small, uncredited work that keeps the unit running, or quietly stops
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the nurse names the specific thing (the re-stocked cart) rather than saying 'good job' — and the orderly visibly registers that someone saw it

exampleSpecs.domain: a high school band director rehearsing a second-chair trumpet player who has been flubbing the same four bars for three weeks
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who supervises someone they privately consider mediocre
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the student keeps showing up to practice or quietly drops the instrument at the end of the semester
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the director locates one real, narrow strength (the kid's phrasing on a slow passage) and says it first, before any correction — without pretending the flubbed bars are fine

exampleSpecs.domain: a small-town landlord standing on a porch to collect rent that is eleven days late from a tenant who has lived there six years
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader about to enter a conversation they already feel morally superior in
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the tenant pays this month and stays, or feels cornered and leaves, and whether the landlord loses a quiet, reliable renter over one hard month
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the landlord chooses between leading with the overdue notice and leading with a true, specific appreciation of the tenant's six-year track record, and the reader sees why the order of those two sentences changes the outcome

exampleSpecs.domain: a retired machinist trying to convince his grown daughter to accept help carrying her groceries up three flights after her surgery
exampleSpecs.audience: a parent of an adult child who refuses help on principle
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the daughter accepts help this week or strains the stitches to prove she doesn't need him
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the father finds something to genuinely admire about her independence and says it before offering the hand — not as a tactic but as a recognition, so the offer no longer sounds like a verdict on her capability

exampleSpecs.domain: a line cook on a Saturday rush noticing that the dishwasher has been silently re-running sauté pans so no station goes without
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who works alongside people whose contribution is easy to overlook
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the dishwasher feels seen enough to stay another month in a job most people quit in two weeks
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: show the shift once where the cook says nothing, and then the same shift where he names the specific thing the dishwasher did; the difference shows up not in words but in how the dishwasher moves on the next Saturday

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional distributor on the phone with a grocer who has just threatened to drop the line over a pricing change
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who negotiates by arguing and is losing accounts without knowing why
exampleSpecs.stakes: a nineteen-year account and the grocer's standing order for the whole county
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the distributor, alone after hanging up, replays the call and finds the exact second where he could have named a real thing he respects about the grocer's business and instead defended the price sheet — and the reader feels the cost of that missed sentence
